html:
Lucy is the partial skeleton of a female Australopithecus afarensis, an early human relative who lived about 3.2 million years ago. It was found in 1974 at Hadar in the Afar region of Ethiopia. Its catalogue number is AL 288-1, and in Ethiopia she is called Dinkinesh, "you are marvellous".

Donald Johanson and his student Tom Gray spotted the first bone on 24 November 1974. The team recovered several hundred pieces, about 40 percent of one skeleton, which was rare for a fossil so old. That night at camp they played the Beatles song "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds", and the name stuck.

Why she mattered:

  • Her skull was small, close to an ape's in brain size.
  • Her hip, leg and knee show she walked upright on two legs.
  • So walking upright came long before big brains, a key point in human evolution.

Footprints at Laetoli in Tanzania, made by the same species about 3.7 million years ago, later backed this up. For two decades Lucy was the best-known human ancestor. Older finds have since been made, several of them also in Ethiopia.

She was found in the same year the Ethiopian monarchy fell. The bones are kept at the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa.
